analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour over two years.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the minimum wage by $1 an hour, with 124 cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the federal wage law to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 an hour to $5.65 on January 1, 1999, and to $6.15 on January 1, 2000 [S2] [S3]. About 124 House members, all Democrats or the one Independent, signed on [S4]. It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, which never advanced it, and it expired when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum would have gotten a raise of up to $1 an hour, reaching $6.15 by 2000 [S2] [S3]. Many workers earning slightly above the minimum would also have benefited as wage scales adjusted upward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour in 1999 and $6.15 an hour in 2000, a two-step increase of $1 an hour [S2] [S3].
The increase takes effect on January 1, 1999, so workers would have seen the first raise within months of the bill's introduction [S3].
The change applies to the core federal minimum wage in the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers most hourly workers nationwide [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum-wage wages — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses — would have borne higher payroll costs, and some of that cost could have been passed to customers through higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Higher payroll costs fall hardest on small businesses and labor-intensive industries like restaurants and retail, which could respond by cutting hours, slowing hiring, or raising prices.
Even at $6.15 in 2000, the federal minimum would have remained below its mid-1960s value after adjusting for inflation, so the increase was a partial restoration rather than a full one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A $1-an-hour raise is a meaningful gain for workers paid at the bottom of the wage scale, and the two-year phase-in gave employers time to adjust. The main cost is the standard trade-off economists debate: some low-wage jobs or hours may be reduced as employers absorb higher payroll costs. On balance, the bill was a straightforward, modestly designed wage increase with a clear phase-in, not an ambitious or badly structured proposal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, which never took it up; it died there when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. David Bonior of Michigan, the House Democratic Whip, introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act on March 19, 1998, with more than 100 original cosponsors including Democratic leader Richard Gephardt [S1] [S3].
The bill had 124 cosponsors — 123 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, March 19, 1998 [S1] [S5].
On April 17, 1998, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No markup, no floor vote, and no hearing action appears in the record; the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage labor — restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses — kept their 1998 payroll costs instead of facing a $1-an-hour increase. Minimum-wage workers received no federal raise, which stayed at $5.15 until 2007.

for.name: Rep. David E. Bonior
for.role: U.S. Representative (MI-05), House Democratic Whip; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 1998 and recruited a large slate of original cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 19, 1998, and sent it to the Workforce Protections subcommittee on April 17, 1998; never scheduled a markup or a vote, and the bill died in committee [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority-party floor leaders of the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill or any standalone minimum wage increase for a House floor vote in 1998, despite the bill's 124 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 124 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee of jurisdiction never advanced the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The most minimum-wage-dependent major industry would have faced a $1-an-hour increase in wage floors for its large hourly workforce. Blocking the bill preserved existing labor costs; the cost of the raise, had it passed, would have fallen partly on prices and partly on payrolls.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Businesses that pay at or near the federal minimum would have borne higher payroll costs phased in over two years. Inaction kept the wage floor at $5.15, which had not been raised since 1997.
The bill's intended beneficiaries lost the chance at a $1-an-hour raise when it died in committee; the federal minimum stayed at $5.15 for years afterward.
